issues.legal_issue: The disputed powers of attorney and sale deeds were proved to have been executed by the property owner, and the evidence did not establish fraud or forgery.
material_facts: The challenged documents were registered, and the owner denied executing them and alleged fraud and forgery.
A deed writer called by the owner testified that he prepared the documents on her instructions, read them to her, and saw her sign them; he was not declared hostile.

A witness to one sale deed testified that the owner executed it in his presence. The signature of a deceased attesting witness was identified by other witnesses and supported by handwriting-expert evidence.
The handwriting experts gave conflicting opinions about the owner’s signatures, and other witnesses supported execution of the documents.
The owner did not produce tangible evidence proving impersonation or fraud, and did not independently prove that the consideration for the challenged sale had not been received.
issues.conclusion: The disputed 1990 power of attorney and sale deeds were proved to have been executed by the owner; the allegations of fraud and forgery were not established.
issues.legal_principle: A registered document is presumed validly executed, and the person challenging it bears the initial burden of rebutting that presumption (Prem Singh v. Birbal). Under Sections 68, 69 and 71 of the Evidence Act, execution of an attested document is proved through an attesting witness, or, where none can be found, through the prescribed handwriting evidence; other evidence may be used when an attesting witness denies or cannot recollect execution. The definition of attestation in Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act requires the witnesses to attest in the manner stated there. Section 71 is to be applied strictly, consistently with Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini. A vendee’s signature is not essential to a sale deed (Aloka Bose v. Parmatma Devi). Evidence given long after an event should not be assessed with a hypersensitive approach to minor discrepancies (Damodar v. State of Rajasthan). Expert opinion is not binding by itself and must be considered with the other evidence; the civil standard is preponderance of probabilities.

rule.if: civil_document_fraud_dispute and registered_documents_challenged and execution_supported_by_scribe_or_attesting_evidence and corroborating_evidence_supports_execution and challenger_lacks_tangible_evidence_of_fraud

predicates.civil_document_fraud_dispute: A party to a civil property dispute alleges that an instrument affecting property was obtained by fraud or forgery.
predicates.registered_documents_challenged: The instruments whose execution is disputed were registered.
predicates.execution_supported_by_scribe_or_attesti: A deed writer or attesting witness gave evidence supporting the alleged executant’s execution of the instruments.
predicates.corroborating_evidence_supports_executio: Other witnesses or documentary evidence corroborated the evidence supporting execution.
predicates.challenger_lacks_tangible_evidence_of_fr: The party alleging fraud did not produce tangible evidence establishing fraud or forgery.

issues.definition: When registered instruments are challenged in a civil property-document fraud dispute, evidence supporting execution and corroborating evidence, together with the absence of tangible proof of fraud, supports treating the instruments as executed and the fraud allegation as unproved.

issues.legal_issue: A party alleging fraud does not shift the burden of proof merely by asserting a relationship of trust or active confidence.
material_facts: The owner and the other family members had cordial relations, and she visited them regularly.
Two family members cultivated land jointly held with the owner, continuing a practice begun while their father was alive.
The owner asserted that the family members enjoyed her trust, but did not prove that they had misused a position of active confidence.
issues.conclusion: The owner did not establish active confidence or its misuse, so the burden of proving the alleged fraud remained on her.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act, the party asserting a fact ordinarily bears the burden of proving it. Section 111 applies when the bona fides of a transaction are in question and a relationship of active confidence is established; the relationship and active confidence must be proved, not merely pleaded. Anil Rishi v. Gurbaksh Singh holds that a fiduciary relationship or dominant position requires tangible proof before the burden shifts.

rule.if: civil_fraud_claim and claimant_asserts_active_confidence and relationship_or_shared_activity_is_shown and tangible_proof_of_active_confidence_or_its_misuse_is_absent

predicates.civil_fraud_claim: A party in a civil dispute alleges that another party committed fraud.
predicates.claimant_asserts_active_confidence: The party alleging fraud claims that the other party held a position of active confidence.
predicates.relationship_or_shared_activity_is_shown: The parties had a close relationship or engaged in shared activities relevant to the dispute.
predicates.tangible_proof_of_active_confidence_or_i: The party alleging fraud did not produce tangible evidence establishing active confidence or its misuse.

issues.definition: When a civil fraud claimant relies on a relationship or shared activities but lacks tangible proof of active confidence or its misuse, the burden of proving fraud remains with that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: A decades-old document may be presumed duly executed when the statutory conditions for the presumption apply and the presumption is not rebutted.
material_facts: A power of attorney executed more than thirty years earlier bore the owner’s signatures.
The owner acknowledged being taken to the relevant office after her father’s death but gave evasive answers when confronted with the document.
The parties acted on the document’s terms from the time it was made, and the owner did not lead evidence to rebut the presumption of due execution.
issues.conclusion: The older power of attorney was properly treated as genuine and binding on the owner.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits a court to presume due execution and attestation of a document that is thirty years old when produced from proper custody. Under Section 4, a ‘may presume’ presumption is rebuttable; the court may regard the fact as proved unless disproved or call for proof. The owner’s failure to rebut the presumption, together with the parties’ conduct under the document, supported treating it as genuine.

predicates.civil_document_validity_dispute: A party to a civil dispute challenges the validity of a document.
predicates.document_is_at_least_thirty_years_old: The document was at least thirty years old when produced in court.
predicates.document_is_produced_from_custody_the_co: The document was produced from custody that the court accepted as proper in the circumstances.
predicates.party_challenging_document_does_not_rebu: The party challenging the document did not produce evidence rebutting due execution.

issues.definition: If a sufficiently old document is produced from custody accepted by the court and the challenger does not rebut due execution, the court may treat it as duly executed and binding.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that fraud delayed the start of limitation fails when the claimant does not prove the alleged fraud.
material_facts: The owner filed suits challenging instruments executed years earlier and asserted that she learned of them after a family gathering and subsequent enquiries.
The courts found that the owner had executed the disputed documents, so the alleged fraud was not established.
The suits were brought beyond the ordinary limitation period applicable from execution of the documents.
issues.conclusion: Section 17 of the Limitation Act did not extend limitation because fraud was not proved, and the suits were barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Limitation Act postpones the start of limitation in specified cases involving fraud or concealed documents until discovery, or until discovery could have occurred with reasonable diligence. Its application requires the claimant to plead and prove both the existence of fraud and its discovery. Because fraud was not established, the claimant could not rely on Section 17.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_property_documents: A civil suit seeks relief concerning the validity or effect of documents affecting property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_fraud_to_postpone_lim: The claimant relies on alleged fraud as the reason limitation should begin later.
predicates.alleged_fraud_is_not_proved: The claimant fails to establish the alleged fraud.
predicates.suit_is_brought_after_ordinary_limitatio: The suit is brought after the ordinary limitation period measured without postponement for fraud.

issues.definition: A claimant who relies on fraud to postpone limitation cannot avoid the ordinary limitation period when the alleged fraud is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising second-appellate jurisdiction cannot reverse concurrent factual findings merely by reappreciating evidence and preferring another possible view.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court made concurrent findings on execution of the disputed documents and the alleged fraud.
The lower courts’ findings were supported by evidence and represented a possible view of the facts.
The High Court reappreciated the evidence and reversed those findings on grounds the Supreme Court found to rest on surmise and conjecture.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the proper limits of second-appellate jurisdiction by disturbing the concurrent factual findings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines a second appeal to a substantial question of law and does not permit the High Court to reverse a lower appellate court’s factual findings merely because another view is possible. Satya Gupta v. Brijesh Kumar states that reversal on facts requires more than reappreciation of evidence and preference for another possible view.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings_are_supporte: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual findings, and evidence supports those findings.
predicates.findings_represent_a_possible_view: The concurrent findings are a possible view of the evidence.
predicates.high_court_reverses_them_by_reappreciati: The High Court reverses the findings by reappreciating evidence without a sufficient legal basis beyond preferring another possible factual view.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, supported concurrent factual findings that represent a possible view cannot be reversed merely because the High Court reappreciates the evidence and prefers another view.

issues.legal_issue: The bona fides of purchasers who acquired property through an attorney need not be doubted when the attorney’s authority is proved and the purchasers checked the registered authority before purchase.
material_facts: The purchasers said that before acquiring a plot they checked the title documents and verified the registered power of attorney at the registration office.
The court found that the power of attorney on which the sale was based had been proved.
The court found no reason to doubt the purchasers’ bona fides.
issues.conclusion: The bona fides of the subsequent purchasers were not open to doubt on the established facts.
issues.legal_principle: The court concluded that there was no reason to doubt the purchasers’ bona fides once the power of attorney authorising the sale had been proved; the purchasers’ stated verification of the registered authority supported that conclusion.

predicates.civil_property_purchase_dispute: A civil dispute concerns a purchase of property made through an attorney.
predicates.attorney_authority_is_proved: The instrument authorising the attorney to deal with the property is proved.
predicates.purchasers_checked_registered_authority_: The purchasers checked the registered authority before completing the purchase.

issues.definition: When the attorney’s authority is proved and purchasers checked the registered authority before buying, their bona fides are not doubted.
